A person with type 2 diabetes attends routine review and has no urinary symptoms.

Why is urine albumin assessment performed?

options.A: To screen for asymptomatic urinary tract infection
options.B: To measure the blood glucose level directly
options.C: To diagnose acute appendicitis at an early stage
options.D: To determine the patient's ABO blood group
options.E: To detect diabetic kidney disease early

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. To detect diabetic kidney disease early
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Urinary albumin assessment is used to detect albuminuria, an important marker of diabetic kidney disease.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Urinary albumin does not detect infection, and asymptomatic bacteriuria is not screened for in this setting. B. Blood glucose is measured using blood tests. C. Appendicitis is diagnosed clinically with appropriate investigation when indicated. D. Blood grouping requires a blood sample.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In diabetes, the urine albumin:creatinine ratio is checked at least annually to detect early kidney disease, when treatment such as an ACE inhibitor or ARB can slow progression.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Type 2 diabetes ↓ Routine review, no urinary symptoms ↓ Albuminuria is an early marker of nephropathy ↓ E, detect diabetic kidney disease early
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, screening for asymptomatic UTI — tempting because it is a urine test, but albumin measurement detects nephropathy, not infection.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Urine albumin testing in diabetes screens for early diabetic kidney disease.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 63-year-old man with diabetes attends his annual review. His feet are intact with no ulceration. What is an important routine preventive measure?

options.E: Cutting calluses with a blade at home

live_plab_copy.why_correct: NICE NG19 recommends regular (at least annual) diabetic foot assessment to detect neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease and deformity, so that risk can be stratified and ulceration prevented.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Walking barefoot increases the risk of unnoticed injury in a neuropathic foot. B. Poorly fitting footwear increases pressure and the risk of ulceration. C. live_plab_copy.pearl: Every person with diabetes needs at least annual foot assessment for neuropathy, ischaemia and deformity, with risk stratification; an active ulcer or infection needs urgent referral.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Diabetes at annual review ↓ Feet currently intact ↓ Neuropathy and ischaemia can develop silently ↓ Detect risk before ulceration ↓ Regular diabetic foot assessment
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, cutting calluses at home — removing callus does reduce pressure, but self-cutting with a blade risks wounds and infection; callus should be managed by a podiatrist.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Examine diabetic feet at least annually to prevent ulceration.

A patient with longstanding diabetes is attending routine retinal screening despite having no visual symptoms.

Why is this important?

options.A: It detects early cataract before it starts to affect the vision
options.B: Retinopathy may be asymptomatic before visual loss occurs
options.C: It replaces the need for annual HbA1c testing and foot checks
options.D: It checks for open-angle glaucoma caused by long-term diabetes

live_plab_copy.thinking: Longstanding diabetes ↓ No visual symptoms ↓ Retinopathy is silent until advanced ↓ Screening detects it early enough to treat ↓ Retinopathy may be asymptomatic
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, checks for glaucoma — diabetes is linked with glaucoma, but the screening programme photographs the retina for diabetic retinopathy and maculopathy, not glaucoma.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Diabetic eye screening finds silent retinopathy before vision is lost.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes develops DKA after an episode of infection. Which factor commonly precipitates DKA?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Infection is a common precipitant of DKA because physiological stress increases insulin requirements and promotes ketogenesis.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Cataract is unrelated. B. Presbycusis is unrelated. D. Stable osteoarthritis does not usually precipitate DKA. E. Mild seasonal rhinitis alone is not a typical major precipitant.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Infection is one of the commonest precipitants of DKA, alongside missed insulin doses and new diagnosis; always look for and treat the underlying trigger.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Type 1 diabetes ↓ DKA after an episode of infection ↓ Stress hormones raise insulin requirement ↓ Relative insulin deficiency drives ketogenesis ↓ Acute infection
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, mild seasonal rhinitis — it sounds like a minor illness, which tempts, but it is not a significant physiological stress; acute infection is the classic DKA trigger.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Infection and missed insulin are classic DKA triggers.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient presents with diabetic ketoacidosis. Their serum potassium is initially 5.8 mmol/L.

Which statement is most appropriate?

options.A: Potassium should not be added to the fluids at any point in this admission
options.B: The serum potassium accurately reflects total-body potassium stores
options.C: Total-body potassium is increased, so calcium gluconate should be given
options.D: Insulin will raise the serum potassium further, so insulin should be delayed
options.E: Total-body potassium is usually low despite a normal or high serum level

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Total-body potassium is usually low despite a normal or high serum level
live_plab_copy.why_correct: In DKA, acidosis and insulin deficiency move potassium out of cells while osmotic diuresis causes losses, so total-body potassium is depleted even when serum potassium is normal or raised; it falls with insulin treatment.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Potassium replacement is usually needed: once serum potassium is 5.5 mmol/L or below, potassium chloride is added to the IV fluids because insulin will drive the level down. B. Serum potassium does not reflect total-body stores in DKA. C. Total-body potassium is usually depleted, not increased, and a level of 5.8 mmol/L does not need calcium gluconate in the absence of ECG changes. D. Insulin moves potassium into cells and lowers serum potassium.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In DKA, serum potassium is often normal or high at presentation despite total-body depletion; it falls once insulin starts, so monitor it closely and replace it in the fluids as the protocol directs.
live_plab_copy.thinking: DKA with potassium 5.8 mmol/L ↓ Acidosis and insulin lack shift potassium out of cells ↓ Osmotic diuresis causes urinary losses ↓ Total-body potassium low despite high serum level
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, serum potassium reflects total-body stores — tempting as the number looks reassuring, but the shift out of cells masks a total-body deficit that insulin will unmask.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: In DKA, serum potassium may be high, but total-body potassium is low.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A conscious patient with diabetes has symptomatic hypoglycaemia and is able to swallow safely.

What is the appropriate immediate approach?

options.A: Give intramuscular glucagon 1 mg as first-line treatment
options.B: Give a starchy snack such as toast as the first treatment
options.C: Give intravenous 50% glucose via a peripheral cannula now
options.D: Give fast-acting oral carbohydrate and recheck glucose
options.E: Give a sugar-free drink and recheck in 1 hour

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Give fast-acting oral carbohydrate and recheck glucose
live_plab_copy.why_correct: A conscious patient who can swallow should receive 15–20 g fast-acting oral carbohydrate (e.g. glucose tablets or juice), with glucose rechecked after 10–15 minutes, then longer-acting carbohydrate (JBDS hypoglycaemia guideline).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. IM glucagon is for patients who cannot take oral treatment safely. B. Slower-acting carbohydrate is given after initial fast-acting carbohydrate, not as first treatment. C. IV glucose is not needed when the patient can swallow, and 50% glucose is irritant to veins. E. Sugar-free drinks contain no glucose, and 1 hour is too long to wait for a recheck.
live_plab_copy.pearl: If the person can swallow safely, fast-acting oral carbohydrate is first-line; recheck glucose after 10–15 minutes and follow with longer-acting carbohydrate once recovered.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Conscious with symptomatic hypoglycaemia ↓ Able to swallow safely, so the oral route is safe ↓ Fast-acting sugar works quickest ↓ Give fast-acting oral carbohydrate and recheck glucose
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, IM glucagon 1 mg — a familiar hypoglycaemia drug, so it looks decisive. It is reserved for patients who cannot take oral treatment safely; this patient can swallow.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Can swallow: fast sugar by mouth, recheck, then a starchy snack. Cannot swallow: IV glucose or IM glucagon.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient with DKA has been started on appropriate fluid therapy and their potassium is safe for insulin treatment.

What is the purpose of insulin in DKA?

options.A: Suppress ketogenesis and correct the metabolic acidosis
options.B: Rapidly normalise blood glucose within the first hour
options.C: Promote renal water retention to restore volume
options.D: Stimulate glycogen breakdown to raise glucose
options.E: Lower serum potassium as the main treatment aim

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Suppress ketogenesis and correct the metabolic acidosis
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Insulin suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis and increases glucose uptake, which corrects the ketoacidosis and hyperglycaemia in DKA.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Glucose should fall steadily, not be normalised rapidly, and correcting glucose is not the main aim. C. Insulin does not correct dehydration; fluid therapy does. D. Insulin inhibits glycogen breakdown and lowers blood glucose. E. Insulin lowers potassium, but this is a hazard to monitor, not the aim of treatment.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Insulin in DKA is given to switch off ketone production and clear the acidosis; glucose falls as well and should come down steadily, not abruptly.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Insulin deficiency drives lipolysis and ketogenesis ↓ Ketoacids cause the acidosis ↓ Insulin suppresses ketone production ↓ Suppress ketogenesis and correct the metabolic acidosis
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, rapidly normalising glucose within the first hour — tempting as hyperglycaemia is obvious, but rapid falls are unsafe and clearing ketones is the real aim.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: In DKA, insulin treats the ketoacidosis; glucose is not the main target.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient with primary adrenal insufficiency has weakness, weight loss and postural dizziness. Which electrolyte abnormality is typical?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Cortisol and aldosterone deficiency in primary adrenal insufficiency can cause hyponatraemia, often accompanied by hyperkalaemia.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Hypernatraemia is not typical. B. This is not the characteristic pattern. C. Hyperphosphataemia is not the characteristic presentation. D. Hypocalcaemia is not the defining electrolyte abnormality.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Primary adrenal insufficiency classically causes hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia with hyperpigmentation; suspected adrenal crisis needs immediate hydrocortisone without waiting for results.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Primary adrenal insufficiency ↓ Cortisol and aldosterone deficiency ↓ Renal sodium loss with potassium retention ↓ Hyponatraemia
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, hypernatraemia — tempts as the sodium option, but aldosterone deficiency causes salt wasting and a low sodium; hypernatraemia would argue against Addison's disease.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Primary adrenal insufficiency: low sodium, often with high potassium.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient with long-standing diabetes develops dizziness on standing, early satiety and abnormal sweating.

What type of complication could explain these symptoms?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Diabetes can damage autonomic nerves, affecting cardiovascular, gastrointestinal and sweating functions.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Peripheral neuropathy causes sensory loss in the feet rather than postural dizziness, early satiety and sweating abnormalities. C. Nephropathy causes albuminuria and declining renal function, not postural dizziness, early satiety and sweating abnormalities. D. Retinopathy affects vision. E. Macrovascular disease causes coronary, cerebrovascular and peripheral arterial disease, not autonomic symptoms.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy can cause postural hypotension, gastroparesis with early satiety, sweating abnormalities, erectile dysfunction and bladder dysfunction.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Long-standing diabetes ↓ Postural dizziness, early satiety, abnormal sweating ↓ Several autonomic functions affected ↓ A, diabetic autonomic neuropathy
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, peripheral neuropathy — the commonest diabetic neuropathy, but it causes distal sensory loss, not postural dizziness, early satiety or sweating changes.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Postural hypotension, gastroparesis and sweating changes in diabetes: autonomic neuropathy.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A person with diabetes treated with insulin experiences recurrent episodes of hypoglycaemia while driving.

What is the most important principle?

options.A: Keep driving but eat a carbohydrate snack every hour on the road
options.B: Follow DVLA driving requirements and seek medical advice
options.C: Increase the insulin dose to improve overall glycaemic control
options.D: Continue driving provided they recognise warning symptoms early
options.E: Stop glucose checks before driving to reduce the associated anxiety

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Follow DVLA driving requirements and seek medical advice
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Hypoglycaemia can impair consciousness and reaction time, creating a significant road-safety risk. Specific DVLA requirements apply to drivers with diabetes.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Snacking does not prevent impaired consciousness from recurrent hypoglycaemia. C. Increasing insulin would worsen hypoglycaemia and should not be done independently. D. Recurrent hypoglycaemia while driving has specific DVLA implications regardless of awareness. E. Glucose monitoring is required before and during driving for insulin-treated drivers.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Insulin-treated drivers must check glucose before driving and at intervals on long journeys, and must not drive while hypoglycaemic; recurrent hypoglycaemia carries specific DVLA rules.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Insulin-treated diabetes ↓ Recurrent hypoglycaemia while driving ↓ Impaired awareness and road-safety risk ↓ Follow DVLA requirements and seek medical advice
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, continue driving if warning symptoms are recognised — awareness helps, but recurrent hypoglycaemia while driving is a safety issue with DVLA implications regardless.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Hypoglycaemia while driving is a DVLA issue: stop driving and seek review.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient has severe hypercalcaemia.

Which ECG change can occur?

options.D: Complete heart block in every case
options.E: Widespread ST elevation in every case

live_plab_copy.why_correct: Hypercalcaemia classically shortens the QT interval.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Delta waves suggest ventricular pre-excitation. C. Hypocalcaemia is associated with QT prolongation. D. Complete heart block is not the characteristic ECG finding. E. Widespread ST elevation suggests acute pericarditis.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Calcium affects ventricular repolarisation: hypercalcaemia shortens the QT interval and hypocalcaemia prolongs it.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Severe hypercalcaemia ↓ Calcium alters the duration of repolarisation ↓ High calcium shortens the ST segment ↓ Shortened QT interval
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, prolonged QT interval — a familiar electrolyte ECG change, but QT prolongation is seen in hypocalcaemia; high calcium shortens the QT.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: High calcium, short QT; low calcium, long QT.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient drinks very large quantities of water and develops recurrent hyponatraemia. Which condition may cause this?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Excessive water intake can overwhelm renal water-excretion capacity and produce dilutional hyponatraemia.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Phaeochromocytoma causes episodic catecholamine-related symptoms. B. Diabetes insipidus causes excessive dilute urine and usually stimulates increased thirst. D. Hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalaemia. E. Hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcaemia.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Primary polydipsia gives dilute urine with low or low-normal serum sodium, whereas diabetes insipidus gives dilute urine with high-normal sodium; serum sodium helps separate them.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Very large water intake ↓ Recurrent hyponatraemia ↓ Intake exceeds renal water-excretion capacity ↓ Dilutional hyponatraemia ↓ Primary polydipsia
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, Diabetes insipidus — also features heavy drinking and dilute urine, but the water loss drives thirst and tends towards high sodium, not hyponatraemia.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Excess drinking with low sodium suggests primary polydipsia, not diabetes insipidus.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 66-year-old woman has several months of fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain and constipation and is now confused. Serum sodium is low, TSH is markedly raised and free T4 is low. Which endocrine disorder is contributing to her hyponatraemia?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: The raised TSH and low free T4 with typical symptoms indicate primary hypothyroidism, and severe hypothyroidism impairs free-water excretion (reduced cardiac output and GFR, increased ADH effect), causing hyponatraemia.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Hyperthyroidism causes weight loss and heat intolerance with a suppressed TSH and does not characteristically cause hyponatraemia. B. Acromegaly is caused by growth hormone excess and does not explain the raised TSH and low free T4. C. Phaeochromocytoma causes paroxysmal hypertension, sweating and palpitations from catecholamine excess, not hyponatraemia with hypothyroid features. D. Primary hyperaldosteronism causes sodium retention with hypertension and hypokalaemia, and sodium is usually normal or high.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Hypothyroidism is a recognised cause of hyponatraemia, so thyroid function belongs in every hyponatraemia work-up; severe hypothyroidism with confusion should raise concern for myxoedema coma.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation ↓ Raised TSH and low free T4 ↓ Primary hypothyroidism ↓ Impaired free-water excretion ↓ Hypothyroidism causing hyponatraemia
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, Primary hyperaldosteronism — an endocrine cause of electrolyte change, but it retains sodium and causes hypokalaemia, not hyponatraemia.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Always check thyroid function when working up hyponatraemia.

Which complication is of greatest immediate concern?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Severe hyponatraemia can cause cerebral oedema, resulting in neurological deterioration and seizures.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Hyponatraemia does not cause polycythaemia, and diuretic haemoconcentration does not explain the neurological picture. C. options.A: Withhold the steroid until the fever has settled
options.B: Continue the usual dose unchanged during the illness

live_plab_copy.pearl: Steroid-dependent patients cannot raise their own cortisol when ill. During febrile illness they follow sick-day rules (usually doubling the glucocorticoid dose) and need IM or IV hydrocortisone if vomiting or unwell.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Long-term steroid replacement ↓ Cannot mount a stress cortisol response ↓ Febrile illness raises steroid requirement ↓ Under-replacement risks adrenal crisis ↓ Follow sick-day steroid rules in their individual plan
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, continue the usual dose unchanged — tempting because changing nothing feels safe. Illness increases steroid requirements, so the usual dose may be inadequate and risks adrenal crisis.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Steroid-dependent and unwell: increase steroid cover per sick-day rules; never stop it.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient with type 2 diabetes has an HbA1c of 62 mmol/mol.

What does HbA1c primarily reflect?

options.A: Mean blood glucose concentration over the previous 2–3 weeks
options.B: Fasting plasma glucose level on the morning of the test
options.C: Average blood glucose over the previous 2–3 months
options.D: Peak postprandial glucose concentrations over the previous week
options.E: Endogenous insulin secretion over the previous 3 months

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Average blood glucose over the previous 2–3 months
live_plab_copy.why_correct: HbA1c reflects glycation of haemoglobin over the red-cell lifespan, so it indicates average blood glucose over roughly the previous 2–3 months.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Glycaemia over the previous 2–3 weeks is reflected by fructosamine, not HbA1c. B. A fasting plasma glucose measures glucose at a single point in time; HbA1c does not. D. HbA1c reflects average glycaemia, not peak postprandial values. E. HbA1c does not measure insulin secretion; C-peptide is used for that.
live_plab_copy.pearl: HbA1c reflects haemoglobin glycation over the red-cell lifespan, giving average glucose over about 2–3 months; it can mislead when red-cell turnover is altered, such as in haemolysis.
live_plab_copy.thinking: HbA1c is glycated haemoglobin ↓ Glycation accumulates over the red-cell lifespan ↓ Red cells survive about 3 months ↓ Average blood glucose over the previous 2–3 months
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, the previous 2–3 weeks — the figure sounds similar, but that shorter window is reflected by fructosamine, not HbA1c.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: HbA1c reflects average glycaemia over roughly the previous 2–3 months.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient with diabetes has a haemoglobinopathy and HbA1c results do not appear to reflect their measured glucose levels.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Repeat HbA1c monthly until the results agree
options.B: Base treatment on HbA1c, as it is the most reliable measure
options.C: Use a higher HbA1c target to allow for the haemoglobinopathy
options.D: Investigate and consider an alternative glycaemic measure
options.E: Intensify glucose-lowering treatment because HbA1c is above target

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Investigate and consider an alternative glycaemic measure
live_plab_copy.why_correct: HbA1c may be unreliable in haemoglobinopathies or altered red cell turnover, so discrepancies should be investigated and alternative measures such as capillary glucose monitoring or fructosamine considered (NICE NG28).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Repeating HbA1c does not solve the interference from the haemoglobinopathy. B. HbA1c may be unreliable in haemoglobinopathies and should not be relied upon here. C. Adjusting the target does not correct an unreliable measurement. E. Intensifying treatment based on an unreliable HbA1c risks hypoglycaemia.
live_plab_copy.pearl: When HbA1c and glucose readings disagree, suspect interference from a haemoglobin variant or altered red cell turnover and use another measure such as capillary glucose or fructosamine.
live_plab_copy.thinking: HbA1c can be unreliable when erythrocyte turnover or haemoglobin characteristics interfere with measurement.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, intensify treatment because HbA1c is above target — follows the number, but in a haemoglobinopathy HbA1c may not reflect true glycaemia, so this risks hypoglycaemia.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: When HbA1c does not match glucose readings, question the test before changing treatment.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient with a known pituitary tumour develops fatigue and weight gain. Thyroid testing shows low free T4 with a low or inappropriately normal TSH. What is the most likely diagnosis?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Pituitary or hypothalamic disease can cause low thyroid hormone with a TSH that is low or inappropriately normal rather than appropriately elevated.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Thyroid storm is severe acute thyrotoxicosis. B. Primary hypothyroidism usually causes an elevated TSH. C. Graves disease causes hyperthyroidism. D. Hyperthyroidism produces raised thyroid hormone levels.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In pituitary disease TSH is unreliable, so free T4 must be measured; low free T4 with a low or normal TSH means central hypothyroidism. Assess cortisol before starting levothyroxine.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Known pituitary tumour ↓ Hypothyroid symptoms ↓ Low free T4 ↓ TSH low or inappropriately normal, not raised ↓ Central hypothyroidism
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, Primary hypothyroidism — the symptoms fit, but primary thyroid failure raises TSH; a TSH that is not raised points to the pituitary.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Low free T4 without a raised TSH points to central hypothyroidism.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient has:

- TSH: raised
- Free T4: low

What pattern is present?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: A raised TSH with low free T4 indicates failure of the thyroid gland itself, with appropriate pituitary feedback, i.e. primary hypothyroidism.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Diabetes insipidus relates to ADH, not thyroid function. B. Primary hyperthyroidism shows low TSH with high free T4 or T3. D. TSH and free T4 are both abnormal. E. Hyperparathyroidism affects calcium and PTH, not TSH and T4.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Read thyroid tests as a feedback loop: high TSH with low T4 means the gland is failing while the pituitary pushes harder, i.e. primary hypothyroidism. A low or inappropriately normal TSH with low T4 points to a pituitary (secondary) cause.
live_plab_copy.thinking: TSH raised ↓ Free T4 low ↓ Pituitary is responding appropriately to low hormone ↓ The thyroid gland itself is failing ↓ Primary hypothyroidism
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, primary hyperthyroidism — tempting if a high TSH is misread as an overactive thyroid. Primary hyperthyroidism shows a low TSH with high free T4 or T3.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: High TSH with low T4 = primary hypothyroidism; TSH moves opposite to thyroid output.
